source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: experience-following behavior
finding: Adding every executed experience to an agent memory (add-all) is worse than a fixed small memory on all four agents. Selective addition with a strict evaluator is best on all four. A weak (coarse) evaluator gives gains in between.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, 4 agents. Success/acc, fixed vs add-all vs strict: RegAgent 67.53 / 55.48 / 70.95; EHRAgent 16.75 / 13.05 / 38.50; AgentDriver 40.11 / 32.32 / 51.00; CIC-IoT 71.50 / 59.90 / 85.40. Coarse C1..C3 on EHRAgent 26.19 / 32.21 / 34.66. Memory size under add-all 1,050 to 4,100 entries vs about 900 to 2,900 under strict.
limits: Tasks are single-step prediction-style agents (regression, EHR code, driving, network traffic), not multi-step reasoning. The evaluator uses ground-truth error or a judge. No replay of stored items, only gating of what is written.
agent_relevance: Strongest measured case for a write gate on the subgoal library: unfiltered self-generated traces hurt by 3 to 12 points versus a fixed memory; filtered ones help by 3 to 22 points. Matches the hallucinated-value worry for Dyna.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) deletion results (Table 2 and 4)
finding: Deleting stored items helps only when the evaluator is good. History-based deletion (drop items retrieved at least n times with low average utility) helped on three of four agents with the strict evaluator; periodic deletion shrank memory about 3x but often lost accuracy. With a coarse evaluator deletion often hurt.
numbers: Strict evaluator, none vs history deletion: EHRAgent 38.67 vs 42.06; CIC-IoT 85.40 vs 89.60; AgentDriver 51.00 vs 51.81; RegAgent 70.95 vs 69.80. Periodic deletion RegAgent 70.95 to 67.65 (memory 2938 to 949). Coarse C1 + combined deletion CIC-IoT 74.00 to 68.80. Deleted records were less correct than retained: EHRAgent 36.3 vs 44.1 (4o-mini judge).
limits: Same four agents; thresholds tuned per agent. Retained-vs-deleted gap is a judge-based quality score, not ground truth for utility.
agent_relevance: Gives a first priority signal for a library: retrieval count times average outcome (a need-and-utility score) works as a deletion rule, but only if outcomes are checked. Not a test of replay order.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) error propagation and misaligned replay (Figs 3, 6, 15-16)
finding: With add-all or weak selection the gap to an error-free memory widens over time (error propagation). Even among stored items that look correct, some give little or misleading help when reused (misaligned replay). Strict selection plus deletion eventually passes the error-free run on AgentDriver.
numbers: AgentDriver strict addition passes the ground-truth-memory run after about 2,000 executions; combined deletion + strict passes around task 1,000. Exact curves are figures only; no per-point numbers in the text.
limits: Qualitative from figures. The error-free comparator is a different memory policy, not a different compute budget.
agent_relevance: Names the two failure modes for any library that learns from its own output: propagation of bad entries and reuse of entries that were right only for their own case. Supports an outcome-checked write gate and a re-test on reuse.

source: Reddy (2026) Selective Memory Retention for Long-Horizon LLM Agents (TraceRetain)
finding: On clean ALFWorld with gpt-5-mini, simple recency rules (FIFO, K=50) tie a learned retention scorer. Memory helps over none, but retention policy does not matter. Under a controlled stress where 75 percent of writes are failed distractors, FIFO and unbounded memory collapse in retrieval precision while the learned scorer holds.
numbers: Clean T=200: FIFO-K50 190/200 ties TraceRetain-Linear 190/200 (Wilson CIs overlap). No-memory vs memory seed-42 train 87/100 vs 96-97/100; steps 20.98 vs about 10-12. Noisy-write Precision@5: unbounded 20.2% to 12.4%, FIFO 15.8% to 3.8%, TraceRetain-CEM 16.9% to 16.6%. Paired sign test vs no memory under noise: TraceRetain significant, unbounded p=0.065, FIFO p=0.109. (Table layout garbled in text extraction; figures from the prose.)
limits: Single model, single benchmark, n=100 to 200 per condition, the noise is synthetic. Authors say natural ALFWorld streams did not show pollution. Retention features include success, age, access frequency, redundancy.
agent_relevance: Honest negative result for gap 2: recency is enough when the library is clean; outcome-aware scoring matters only when writes are polluted. Do not build a complex priority rule before measuring pollution.

source: Cao et al. (2025) ReMe: dynamic procedural memory for agent evolution
finding: Memory built by distilling success and failure into small keypoints, with validated adds and utility-based pruning, lets a small model beat a larger one with no memory. Retrieving more entries than about five stops helping and then hurts.
numbers: Qwen3-8B + ReMe(dynamic) vs Qwen3-14B no memory 55.03% vs 54.65% (average over the two benchmarks); Qwen3-14B + ReMe vs Qwen3-32B no memory Avg@4 44.66 vs 40.89, Pass@4 63.71 vs 61.52. Keypoint vs trajectory granularity on BFCL-V3 Qwen3-8B: Avg@4 +4.17 vs +2.67 over no memory. Selective vs full addition +3.50 Avg@4, +2.66 Pass@4 (BFCL-V3, Qwen3-8B). Retrieved K saturates then degrades; K=5 chosen. Latency 21.42 s to 23.96 s per task.
limits: Same-group ablations; utility-deletion effect is stated as a further gain with no exact figure in the text I read. LLM-as-judge validation of new entries.
agent_relevance: Independent line to Xiong: write gate and deletion help, and bigger recall hurts. 'Outdated' here means low utility in a non-stationary run, not an explicit stale test.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), ICLR 2026
finding: Offline replay of training traces into an incremental, delta-updated playbook gives large gains on AppWorld. Multi-epoch passes over the same traces add a few points. Full LLM rewrite of the context collapses it.
numbers: AppWorld, DeepSeek-V3.1, average over 4 splits (recomputed from the table): ReAct 42.4; ACE offline w/o reflector or multi-epoch 55.1; w/o multi-epoch 56.8; full ACE 59.4 (+17.0). So replaying the same traces for 5 epochs adds about +2.6. Online ACE 56.1; with offline warmup 59.5. Context collapse: 18,282 tokens at step 60 with accuracy 66.7 fell to 122 tokens and 57.1 next step (no-adaptation baseline 63.7). Offline adaptation used 80.8% / 83.6% fewer input/output tokens than GEPA.
limits: Epochs add tokens, so the +2.6 is not compute-matched against fresh attempts. Ground-truth labels or execution feedback available in the main setting. Authors state ACE may degrade without reliable feedback.
agent_relevance: Closest measured analogue of an offline replay pass over stored traces for a library. Shows both the benefit of repeated passes (+2.6) and the main hazard: whole-library rewriting loses detail, so use small deltas.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) ACE robustness to harmful reflection (Tables 16-17, FiNER)
finding: Corrupted memory updates cost accuracy in a dose-dependent way. Rare corruption is tolerated; corruption every step drives accuracy below the base model. A weaker reflector still helps.
numbers: FiNER, base 70.7. Harmful reflector every X steps: X=1 66.7 (-4.0); X=5 76.1; X=10 77.0; X=25 77.8; X=50 and 100 78.2; none 78.3. Reflector model: GPT-OSS-120B 76.6, DeepSeek-V3.1 78.3, GPT-5.1 78.5.
limits: Injected harm is instructed adversarial text, not natural simulation error. One benchmark.
agent_relevance: Best available number for gap 7: if 1 in 5 updates is wrong the gain shrinks by about 2 points; if every update is wrong the library is worse than none. Sets a tolerance for simulated-outcome updates.

source: Yu et al. (2025) Dyna-Mind: learning to simulate from experience
finding: Across models, higher simulation accuracy goes with higher success. No threshold was tested. Training on search-tree traces with exact simulation (ReSim) reached 96.4 percent on Sokoban and 87.7 percent on ALFWorld.
numbers: Table 2 Sim Score (judge accuracy of imagined next states) vs success. Sokoban: Qwen2.5-7B 0.21 vs 25.8; DeepSeek-V3 0.54 vs 57.0; R1 0.93 vs 96.6; ReSim 1.00 vs 96.4. ALFWorld: 0.18 vs 35.4; 0.35 vs 55.2; R1 0.36 vs 62.5; ReSim 1.00 vs 87.7. Within-model Spearman r between sim score and success 0.46 to 0.96 (R1 Sokoban 0.96). Dyna-Think row 74.0 Sokoban, 63.2 ALFWorld. Dyna-GRPO 82.5 and 92.5.
limits: Same research group as Dyna-Think, different benchmarks than OSWorld. Models differ in more than simulation accuracy, so the cross-model slope is confounded. Judge is another LLM (Qwen3-235B).
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly addressed: on ALFWorld sim 0.35 to 0.36 already goes with 55 to 62 percent success, far under the exact-simulator 87.7, so lookahead helps long before simulation is accurate but is capped by it. No break-even hit rate exists.

source: Chen et al. (2025) DreamGym: scaling agent learning via experience synthesis (Table 1, read as image)
finding: Table 1 column mapping fixed. Order is WebShop, ALFWorld, WebArena; within each, Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B. Training purely on synthetic experiences roughly matches real-data RL on WebShop, is below it on ALFWorld, and beats it on WebArena; adding 5K real transitions after synthetic training beats 80K real transitions in most cells.
numbers: GRPO, 80K real: WebShop 62.1/65.0/66.1, ALFWorld 65.3/70.9/79.8, WebArena 7.3/6.1/6.1. GRPO DreamGym (0 real): WebShop 59.3/63.9/68.3; ALFWorld 62.1/66.3/71.0; WebArena 13.3/9.1/12.7. GRPO DreamGym-S2R (5K): WebShop 70.5/75.0/72.1; ALFWorld 65.0/75.9/82.4; WebArena 13.9/9.7/11.2. PPO 80K: WebShop 59.9/64.2/68.1; ALFWorld 47.0/72.9/81.1; PPO DreamGym 60.5/58.1/65.0; 40.5/70.8/72.7. SFT 20K: WebShop 32.0/35.1/32.9.
limits: Experience model trained from Llama-3.1-8B for all rows. WebArena rates are low (under 15), so differences are a few points. Single group.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 10. Synthetic rollouts alone lost 0.3 to 8.8 points to real GRPO on ALFWorld (Qwen 79.8 vs 71.0) but beat it on WebArena, so simulated experience is a partial substitute, not a free one.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute (pass@k comparison and limits)
finding: The controls compare against test-time tokens only. Sleep-time compute beats pass@k at the same test-time budget, but pass@k needs an oracle verifier and sleep-time tokens are extra. Gains shrink when the query is not predictable from the context.
numbers: Test-time compute for equal accuracy about 5x lower; up to +13% Stateful GSM-Symbolic and +18% Stateful AIME with more sleep-time compute; cost per query 2.5x lower over many related queries. Predictability bins: accuracy gain rises with predictability (five quantile bins, Fig 10).
limits: No comparison at equal total (sleep plus test) tokens. Stateful tasks were built by the authors by splitting a problem into context and query. One group; follow-up replications were not found.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open: the matched-compute control is on test-time tokens only. For our library, offline passes need a total-token ledger before any claim that replay beats a fresh attempt.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory, Mind2Web generalisation (Table 4)
finding: Offline workflows from training examples and online workflows induced from the agent's own (judged) test trajectories perform about the same when train and test match. As the gap widens the online version pulls ahead, because offline routines go stale relative to the test distribution.
numbers: GPT-4 Mind2Web Step SR: cross-task MindAct 36.2, AWM offline 45.1, online 43.6; cross-website 30.1, 33.7, 33.9; cross-domain 18.6, 32.6, 35.5. Whole-task SR cross-domain 1.0, 0.7, 1.7. Abstract: online beats baselines by 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as the gap widens.
limits: Whole-task success rates are 0.7 to 4.8 percent; the gains are in step success. Online workflows come from model-predicted trajectories judged by a model, so wrong ones can enter and degrade the memory (authors' own statement).
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the one measured staleness-like result. A library built on a different distribution loses 2.9 step-SR points to one built on the live one at cross-domain; no explicit stale-detection step is tested.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: A case bank with a learned retrieval policy (soft Q-learning over cases) beats similarity retrieval and no case bank, by small margins that shrink over iterations. The no-bank baseline also rises across iterations.
numbers: DeepResearcher, 5 iterations: w/o CBR 78.65, 82.62, 84.47 (iter 1,3,5); non-parametric CBR 79.84, 83.09, 84.85; parametric (Q-learned) 80.46, 84.10, 85.44. Iter 5 gap learned vs similarity +0.59; vs no CBR +0.97. GAIA val 87.88 Pass@3, test 79.40; OOD +4.7 to +9.6 points. Authors report no performance drops along the curve; bank saturates with about 3k training items.
limits: Small gaps, single runs, no CIs. Q-learning on case utility is a learned value, not replay by prediction error. Case bank stores failures too.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: utility-learned case selection is slightly better than similarity, but the effect is under 1 point; the cheap rule is nearly as good. Failures stored with successes cause no measured harm here.

source: Moore and Atkeson (1993) Prioritized Sweeping, Machine Learning 13, Table 2 (primary text, table read as image)
finding: Verified. Prioritised sweeping needs fewer real observations than Dyna with the same backup budget in almost all mazes, and about half the wall-clock time. At 300 backups per observation the gap grows.
numbers: Observations to 98% optimal decisions, stochastic mazes, 2627-state: PriSweep 94,000; Dyna-opt 155,000; Dyna-PI+ 240,000. 4528-state: 200,000 / 310,000 / 525,000. Deterministic 2627-state: PriSweep 29,000; Dyna-opt 105,000; Dyna-PI+ 195,000. 4528-state deterministic: 59,000 / 245,000 / over 10^6. 4528-state with 300 backups: Dyna-opt 143,000 obs and 3 hours; PriSweep 21,000 obs and 15 minutes. Exceptions: 15-state stochastic PriSweep 600 vs Dyna-PI+ 400; 15-state deterministic PriSweep 150 vs Dyna-opt 300 but 117-state deterministic PriSweep 1,200 vs Dyna-opt 900. Table 3: Dyna-PI+ 252 vs PriSweep 472 on one small problem.
limits: Tabular mazes, backup budget 10 per observation, optimism heuristic tuned (r_opt=200, T_bored=1 or 5). Mostly one run per cell, authors say variance was small.
agent_relevance: Closes the maze-number part of gap 9. Priority ordering matters most with large state spaces and a tight backup budget; on small problems a simple sweep is as good.

source: Zhang, Kahn, Daw, Nussenbaum, Hartley (2026) Children leverage predictive representations for flexible, value-guided choice. Cognition
finding: An independent group adapted the Momennejad revaluation task for ages 7 to 23. Reward revaluation produced replanning in both rest and no-rest versions, but a 60-second rest did not increase replanning. This is a null on the rest-aids-planning link, with a changed design.
numbers: Exp 1 n=119 (60 s active rest): revaluation effect on replanning estimate -0.06 [-0.10,-0.02], p=.008. Exp 2 n=119 (no rest): -0.11 [-0.15,-0.06], p<.001. Block x experiment (rest effect) -0.02 [-0.06,0.01], p=.13 (trend in the wrong direction). Exp 3 n=152 SR test: SR signature log-odds 0.12, p<.001; children alone 0.09, p=.002; model weights MB 0.59, SR 0.41, MF 0.40.
limits: Between-experiment comparison, active-rest distractor task (red dots), rest of 60 s, no Bayes factors, no effect sizes beyond log-odds. Not a direct replication of the fMRI replay-replanning correlation. Discussion section not read in full.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: first outside evidence that rest-time replay may not be needed for revaluation; reactivation during relearning could suffice. Weakens the claim that a separate offline pass is the key ingredient.

source: Kahn and Daw (2025) Humans rationally balance detailed and temporally abstract world models. Commun Psychol
finding: Humans mix successor-representation and model-based learning, and shift toward the SR when future states are predictable. This is a second independent line on the SR-versus-MB question, with no replay.
numbers: n=100 analysed (104 recruited), 200 trial pairs. Mixture weights: beta_MB 0.88, beta_SR 0.866, beta_TD 0.369. SR weight after congruent changes 0.604 [0.496,0.705] vs after incongruent 0.336 [0.197,0.504]; difference p<0.006; 93 of 100 subjects in the predicted direction. No AIC/BIC reported.
limits: Trial-by-trial learning task, not train-revalue-probe. The text does not mention replay.
agent_relevance: Supports the hybrid reading (K05): neither pure SR nor pure model-based. Suggests an agent should lean on cached summary values when the task family is predictable and re-simulate when it is not.

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Between planning and map building: prioritising replay when future goals are uncertain. Neuron
finding: Extends the Mattar and Daw expected-value-of-backup theory to weight future goals by their likelihood of relevance. Replay then looks like planning when the current goal dominates and like map building when goals are uncertain.
numbers: Abstract only; no figures read.
limits: Abstract level. Theory, no LLM test.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: gives a normative priority of need times gain where need is the chance a goal recurs. For a library, that is expected reuse, supporting reuse-weighted over recency-weighted replay. Untested in LLMs.

source: Antonov and Dayan (2025) Exploring replay. Nat Commun
finding: Extends the replay-priority theory to unknown or changed environments, so replay can choose exploratory sequences. This is the normative form of the Dyna-Q+ idea of re-testing stale model parts.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Abstract level; a model of a spatial task.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: gives a principled answer to what to re-test after change (high uncertainty times high potential gain) but no LLM test exists in what I found.

source: Wang et al. (2026) OEP: poisoning self-evolving LLM agents via locally correct but non-transferable experiences
finding: Self-evolving reflective agents can distil a single locally correct but non-transferable case into a high-priority, over-general rule. Attack success rate above 50 percent with GPT-4o agents across three domains.
numbers: ASR above 50% (GPT-4o), three domains; I read the abstract and introduction only.
limits: Attack paper, adversarially constructed cases. Read in part.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 and 3: shows that consolidation from a single clean case can produce an over-generalised stale rule. Supports keeping rule scope and a re-test count on each library entry.

source: Hazard et al. (2025) SuRe: surprise-driven prioritised replay for continual LLM learning
finding: Surprise (negative log-likelihood) picks which samples enter a replay buffer for continual fine-tuning. It is a weight-update setting, not in-context memory. Full text could not be decoded in this session.
numbers: Not read (PDF streams not decoded). Paper lists 11 tables and compares to experience replay, EWC, O-LoRA.
limits: Abstract-level only; fine-tuning, not scaffold memory.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the only LLM paper found that uses surprise as a replay priority; it does not transfer directly to a no-training scaffold. Not used as evidence.

source: Sutton (1990) Integrated architectures for learning, planning and reacting (ICML)
finding: PDF retrieved but it is an image scan with no text layer, so the maze episode counts were not read. The Moore and Atkeson text confirms how Dyna-PI+ and its exploration bonus (epsilon=0.001) were used.
numbers: Not read.
limits: No OCR available in this session.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays partly open for the Sutton episode counts (5 vs 25 episodes claim in K01 still from secondary text).
